allusion: An allusion is an intended reference: a work calls on its audience to retrieve a specific earlier text, event, or figure, demanding associations that go beyond merely substituting one referent for another. Philosophers of language and literature ask what separates allusion from quotation, plagiarism, or accidental resemblance, and what a work gains when part of its meaning depends on recognizing something never stated outright. On the account used in chapter 6, what makes an allusion succeed or fail is the combination of the creator's intention that the reference be recognized and the associations the recognized source then brings with it.
hypocrisy: Hypocrisy is the vice of acting in deliberate violation of the values one espouses, whether the espousal is explicit or tacit. Philosophers debate where its wrongness lies: in the inconsistency itself, in the self-deception often needed to sustain it, in the unearned claim to moral standing it expresses, or in the contempt it shows for the audience one lectures. On the formal account defended in chapter 12, hypocrisy just is the mismatch between espoused values and deliberate action, with the further question of blame left to particular cases.
